rows.label: Concept
rows.text: **Equipotential surfaces** are loci of constant potential. Their properties: moving a charge along one does **no work** ($W = q\Delta V = 0$); field lines cross them **at right angles** (any tangential field component would change V); two surfaces **never intersect** (one point, two potentials — impossible); crowding marks strong fields; and a conductor's whole interior is a single equipotential region (NEB 2024,…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - W = qΔV = 0 along an equipotential - E ⊥ equipotential surface - Point charge: spheres V = kq/r

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Equipotential ⊥ field lines, always** — the geometry encodes E = −dV/dr.  ·  **Zero work along the surface, not small work** — ΔV = 0 exactly.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Inside a charged conductor there is no field direction, so the concept of perpendicularity does not apply there; the whole cavity is simply at the constant potential of the conductor's surface.  ·  For a dipole, the V = 0 equipotential surface is the perpendicular bisector plane of the axis — the only region in the dipole's field where V is exactly zero, though E is non-zero there.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Parallel plates*** — evenly spaced planes between the plates.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Derive the proof that E is normal to an equipotential surface.  ·  Sketch equipotential diagrams for the three canonical charge distributions.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "List: no work, ⊥ field lines, never intersect, crowded = strong."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Reasoning (2m): Why does a charge move along an equipotential surface with zero work?** — Work = qΔV and ΔV = 0 between any two points of the surface; the field's tangential component is zero, so no force acts along the path.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Pair the answer with a sketch — point-charge spheres and plate planes.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Equipotentials are contour lines of the electric landscape** — closer spacing means steeper potential, stronger field.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: No work along the surface; field ⊥ surface; surfaces never intersect.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The entire interior of a conductor in equilibrium is one equipotential volume — the principle behind Faraday cages.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Walking Uphill Without Effort Move a charge along an equipotential surface and you do no work — like walking along a contour line at constant altitude. Equipotentials turn energy thinking into geometry: where surfaces crowd, fields are strong; where they are flat, nothing pushes.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2024) ### 2.1 Definition **Equipotential surfaces** are surfaces (real or imaginary) over which the electric potential is constant. Every point on one has the same V — a contour map of the electric landscape. ### 2.2 Properties (NEB 2024, 3m) 1. **No work** is done in moving a charge along an equipotential surface ($W = q\,\Delta V = 0$). 2.…  ·  ## 3. Conceptual Relationships - **To Topic 90:** the surface is the locus V = constant of the potential field. - **To Topic 92:** E = −dV/dr — zero component along the surface is the same statement geometrically. - **To conductors:** the entire conductor in equilibrium is one equipotential region.
